title: Terminological Inexactitude: Parliamentary Eloquence
culture_region: India / Greece / USA / South Africa / World
summary: Refusing to retract his condemnation, Churchill rephrased the accusation of lying as 'a terminological inexactitude', legally complying with decorum while driving his point home.
full_text:
Under the strict conventions of the British House of Commons, calling another member a 'liar' is unparliamentary and demands immediate retraction.

In 1906, thirty-two-year-old Winston Churchill was serving as Under-Secretary for the Colonies. During an intense debate regarding indentured labor in South Africa, an opposition member presented misleading statistics.

Churchill leaped to his feet:
"Mr. Speaker, the honorable member's statement is a deliberate lie!"

The Speaker rose sternly:
"The honorable gentleman knows that the word 'lie' is unparliamentary! He must withdraw the expression at once!"

Churchill bowed with impeccable courtliness:
"Mr. Speaker, I gladly withdraw the word.
Allow me to substitute it with the precise parliamentary truth:
The honorable member's statement was perhaps not a lie, but rather...
**A terminological inexactitude!**"

The House erupted in laughter.

'Terminological inexactitude' meant precisely the same thing—a blatant untruth—yet it adhered to the letter of parliamentary law. The phrase entered the English lexicon as one of the most celebrated linguistic inventions of British politics.
moral: Mastery of language allows one to speak uncomfortable truths with precision while respecting institutional decorum.
witty_quote: It could not be described as a lie; it was rather a terminological inexactitude!
